posts.title: A scarf joint without steel
posts.excerpt: Two beams, one long diagonal cut and four oak pegs. Why we still join old timber the way it was first joined.
posts.content:
Steel plates are quick, but wood and steel move differently with the seasons, and water gathers where they meet. A scarf joint lets the new piece move with the old one.

Cutting one takes a full day. Fitting it takes ten minutes, if the day was spent well.

posts.title: Sharpening before sunrise
posts.excerpt: Every morning starts at the water stones. Half an hour, three grits, and a blade that can take a shaving thinner than paper.
posts.content:
The apprentice sharpens first, then Ren checks the edge against his thumbnail. If it skates, the apprentice starts again.

A sharp plane leaves a surface that sheds water and dust. A dull one tears the fibres, and the wood greys within a year.

posts.title: Opening an attic from 1908
posts.excerpt: Under a century of dust: the carpenter’s ink marks still on the rafters, and a beam that needed only its last metre replaced.
posts.content:
We lifted three ceiling boards and climbed in with torches. The roof had been built by someone careful: every rafter numbered, every joint cut to fit only its own place.

The rot was limited to one corner, under a broken gutter. Two weeks of work instead of the new roof the owners had feared.
